blocks.text: Mixture of Experts, MoE, fine-tuning adapts a model architecture where only a subset of its parameters, specific experts selected by a router, actually process each input token, a distinct fine-tuning challenge from the dense models covered in most of this course, since deciding what to fine-tune, all experts, a subset, or just the router, is itself a design choice.

This topic covers how MoE architecture routing works, the specific fine-tuning strategies it enables, and the load balancing challenge that comes with training a router alongside the experts it selects.
1. What an MoE Architecture Looks Like

blocks.alt: An input token goes through a router, which selects expert A and expert B, leaving expert C unused

blocks.text: An MoE model contains many separate expert sub-networks, but a router component selects only a small subset of them, often just one or two, to actually process each input token, rather than routing every token through every expert.
2. Dense Models vs MoE Models

blocks.alt: A dense model activates all parameters while an MoE model activates only selected experts

blocks.text: A standard dense model, covered throughout most of this course, uses all of its parameters for every input, an MoE model instead has a much larger total parameter count but activates only a fraction of them per token, letting it scale total capacity without a proportional increase in per-token compute cost.

blocks.text: 3. What to Fine-Tune in an MoE Model

blocks.alt: Fine-tuning all experts, the router only, or a subset of experts are three distinct strategies

blocks.text: Fine-tuning an MoE model presents a choice not present in dense model fine-tuning, updating all experts, updating only the router that decides which experts handle each token, or updating just a targeted subset of experts, each strategy trades off compute cost against how much the model behavior actually shifts.
4. Applying LoRA to MoE Experts

blocks.alt: LoRA applied per expert produces parameter efficient MoE fine-tuning

blocks.text: The parameter-efficient techniques covered in an earlier module extend naturally to MoE, attaching a LoRA adapter to each expert individually, combining MoE architecture efficiency with the training-time efficiency LoRA already provides for dense models.

blocks.text: 5. The Load Balancing Challenge

blocks.alt: Load imbalance where some experts are overused is compared against balanced routing

blocks.text: During fine-tuning, a router can drift toward relying heavily on just a few experts, leaving others rarely used, this load imbalance wastes model capacity and can degrade quality, MoE training typically includes an auxiliary loss term specifically encouraging the router to distribute tokens more evenly across available experts.

blocks.title: This is a genuinely distinct training concern from anything in dense model fine-tuning
blocks.content: Dense models have no analogous routing decision to worry about, load balancing is a fine-tuning consideration unique to MoE architectures that needs its own dedicated monitoring during training.

blocks.text: 6. Total Parameters vs Active Parameters

blocks.alt: A large total parameter count contrasts with a small active parameter count per token

blocks.text: When discussing MoE model size, it matters whether the total parameter count, including all experts, or the active parameter count, only the experts actually used per token, is being referenced, these can differ by a large factor, and fine-tuning compute and memory planning needs to account for both figures correctly.
7. Router Collapse

blocks.alt: Router collapse, where the same experts are always chosen, leads to a loss of expert diversity

blocks.text: A more severe version of the load balancing problem, router collapse, happens when the router converges to consistently selecting the same small set of experts regardless of input, effectively wasting the unused experts entirely, careful learning rate choice and the load balancing loss covered above both help prevent this failure mode.
8. Fine-Tuning Strategy Selection

Choosing between fine-tuning all experts, a subset, or just the router depends on the available compute budget and how much behavior change the task actually needs, router-only fine-tuning is cheapest but limited to changing routing decisions, full expert fine-tuning is most expensive but can meaningfully shift what each expert has learned.
9. Evaluating an MoE Fine-Tuning Run

Beyond the standard evaluation approaches covered throughout this course, MoE fine-tuning benefits from specifically monitoring expert utilization statistics, confirming the router is distributing load reasonably rather than collapsing toward a small subset, a diagnostic with no direct equivalent in dense model evaluation.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning a large MoE model for a specialized task starts with a limited compute budget and chooses to fine-tune only the router alongside LoRA adapters on a small subset of experts, rather than updating every expert fully.

Monitoring expert utilization statistics throughout training, they catch an early sign of load imbalance, two experts absorbing a disproportionate share of tokens, and adjust their load balancing loss weight to correct it before it worsens into full router collapse, preserving the model ability to use its full expert capacity.
Common Mistakes

items: Not monitoring expert utilization during fine-tuning, missing early signs of load imbalance or router collapse
Confusing total parameter count with active parameter count when planning fine-tuning compute and memory needs
Fully fine-tuning all experts when a cheaper router-only or subset strategy would have met the task needs
Applying dense model fine-tuning intuitions directly without accounting for the MoE-specific routing dynamics

blocks.text: Practice

For an MoE model fine-tuning task you are designing or could imagine, decide between fine-tuning all experts, a subset, or just the router based on your compute budget, and explain what expert utilization monitoring you would put in place to catch load imbalance early.
Key Takeaway

Mixture of Experts fine-tuning must decide what to actually update, all experts, a subset, or just the router, with parameter-efficient techniques like LoRA extending naturally to per-expert adaptation, and it introduces a genuinely new concern absent from dense model fine-tuning, load balancing across experts, requiring dedicated monitoring to avoid router collapse and wasted model capacity.
